analysis.title: Overwhelmed? Goldman's Top Traders Explain The Market Chaos...
key_insights: Goldman's trading desks describe last week as a sharp reassessment of risk across equities, credit and derivatives. Traders moved from celebrating AI-driven growth to questioning the cost of funding it.
Tony Pasquariello says markets have entered a new phase in the AI sequence that is 'unequivocally more complicated', with an intense debate over both the availability and the cost of capital.
AI credit spreads have widened to the worst levels of the year. The AI leaders-vs-laggards basket has given back all its gains from the first half of 2026.
The gap between high- and low-quality assets is widening across both credit and equities, reinforcing a defensive shift toward quality and balance sheet strength.

Mark Wilson (credit) says AI-related bonds from neoclouds or issuers with frontier lab exposure are at the epicentre of the funding cost debate. The trigger was scrutiny of AI funding models, CoreWeave-related commentary, and debate over frontier lab economics and value capture.

Wilson argues the debate should not be confused with a collapse of the AI thesis, saying the mega-theme of AI development and investment is 'very much intact'. He cites OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar saying 'we're still short compute' as evidence that demand remains robust.

Lee Coppersmith says Friday showed 'the first real sign of panic in index protection'. VIX futures volume was 3.6x normal, CBOE index put volume hit an all-time record, and VIX call activity was the second-highest in five years.

Dealer gamma moved substantially lower and hedge funds cut risk. Prime data showed US long/short net leverage falling 3.2 percentage points, the largest weekly decline since Liberation Day. Global Tech saw its largest percentage net selling on record since 2016.

Managers mostly added shorts rather than exiting longs, so portfolios are more defensive but not capitulating. Coppersmith concludes the market is moving into a different volatility environment but not necessarily a more bearish one.
Peter Callahan notes the Nasdaq had its worst week since Liberation Day, led by semiconductors, which posted their longest losing streak since 2008.

Unlike July's purely technical momentum unwind, this decline has triggered a genuine debate over the durability of the AI growth story. Investors disagree on the primary overhang into year-end: earnings, elections, rates, credit, inflation, product momentum or AI build-out execution.
Semiconductors have de-rated from roughly 29x forward earnings this summer to 17x. The Nasdaq trades near its lowest multiple since the AI cycle began in 2023.

Louis Miller argues investors should 'buy the broadening'. AI beneficiaries are down roughly 25% from their highs, but SPX ex-AI has substantially outperformed the headline index, quality factors are at new highs, and non-AI growth continues to attract capital.
Miller's team favours quality, healthcare and selected international opportunities and describes the environment as rotation rather than market-wide deterioration.

Brian Garrett says US long/short net exposure is at five-year lows and sentiment has deteriorated sharply, but breadth is improving. About 350 S&P constituents rose last week and SPX ex-AI outperformed by nearly 500bps.
Garrett says the next move depends more on earnings confirmation than anything else. 14% of the S&P reports this week and another 44% the following week.

Goldman's synthesis is that markets are debating how AI should be financed, who captures the value and what returns justify the investment scale. The market has shifted from a momentum-driven phase to a fundamentally driven one.
